implementation_notes: GCD's DispatchGroup is the countdown latch: enter() before starting each unit of work (or the group-aware async methods that pair enter and leave automatically), leave() on every exit path, and wait(timeout:) or notify(queue:) to observe completion - notify is the non-blocking form and the only one safe on the main queue. GCD ships no reusable phase barrier: the barrier flag on DispatchWorkItem is a mutual-exclusion flag that drains a concurrent queue, not a rendezvous, so a phase barrier must be composed from a semaphore plus an arrival counter or from a serial coordination queue.
pitfalls: leave() must be called exactly once per enter(): a return or thrown error that skips it leaves wait() blocking until its timeout, while an extra leave() unbalances the group and can crash.
DispatchQueue barrier flags are not rendezvous: using a .barrier work item as a phase barrier yields mutual exclusion against a concurrent queue, not group alignment.
wait() on the main thread deadlocks the UI (the main queue cannot service the work being waited for); use notify(queue:) or a background context instead.

variants.name: TaskGroup (structured concurrency)
variants.idiom_name: withTaskGroup / withThrowingTaskGroup + for await in group
variants.implementation_notes: Swift's structured concurrency gives the latch a language-level form: withTaskGroup (or withThrowingTaskGroup) creates a scope that cannot exit before every added child task finished, so the closing brace is the fan-in point and `for try await partial in group` streams results as they complete - the arrival-order collect that a latch approximates. Cancellation of the parent task propagates into the group automatically. There is still no reusable phase barrier primitive in Swift, so multi-phase alignment must be built from continuations or an actor holding an arrival counter.
pitfalls: TaskGroup children must not outlive the scope: escaping a task handle is a compile error, and a child that ignores cancellation stalls the group's exit, so cancellation checks belong inside the child.
Group iteration order is completion order, not submission order: code that needs positional results must carry an identifier in the result type instead of relying on the sequence.
A throwing task cancels siblings but the group still waits for them to observe cancellation; if a child blocks on non-cancellable work the group hangs despite the error.
